certainty_reasoning: Wilde's own words, and only Wilde's: Le Gallienne's side of the correspondence is not in this volume, so the record is one-sided by survival. What follows from it is not recorded, hence `outcome: unknown`.
summary: Wilde wrote to Richard Le Gallienne over about ten years, mostly about books. In December 1890, thanking him for his study of Meredith, the register changed: he asked when they could meet, named what was between them as friendship and love, and finished on his laurels being too thick to kiss beneath. Le Gallienne's replies are not in the volume, so what came of it is not on the record.

sources.quote: I want so much to see you: when can that be? Friendship and love like ours need not meetings, but they are delightful. I hope your laurels are not too thick across your brow for me to kiss your eyelids. Always yours OSCAR
sources.context: The close of Wilde's letter to Le Gallienne postmarked 1 December 1890, from 16 Tite Street, praising his George Meredith: Some Characteristics, published a fortnight before. The preceding paragraph is literary criticism of the ordinary extravagant kind; the last paragraph is not.
sources.supports: The class, and the direction - this is Wilde writing, and only Wilde.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
